entries.clue: Leader in Sun, Farage: "Our NHS needs Reform". Such a divisive character! (5,8)

indicatorNotes.Leader in: a leader is the one out in front, so the letter wanted is the one at the front of the word named after it
indicatorNotes.needs Reform: a party name in the surface, but to reform a thing is to give it a new shape, and letters reshaped come out in another order

blocks.note: the front letter of the newspaper's name, and the only letter taken from it
six letters for the mix, the surname as it stands
six more letters for the mix, the slogan taken as written

annotation.surface: A Sun editorial quoting Farage on Reform and the health service, with a sigh about someone who splits opinion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader' beside a newspaper wants to be the editorial column, and is a single letter. Every political word inside the quotation marks is raw material, and the person who comes out of it is a royal rather than a politician.
annotation.definitionFit: Sarah Ferguson, Duchess of York, has divided British opinion between affection and scorn for forty years, which is what makes her a divisive character.

entries.clue: Time for another bit to eat? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is plural and 'Time' is a mass noun: the setter defines the counted units by the stuff they measure, which is how a clock face is read.

blocks.note: sixty of them to the minute, the units a watch counts off
a second helping, asked for once the first plate is empty

annotation.surface: Somebody wondering whether there is time to eat something more.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the helping sense as table talk rather than a dictionary's leading entry. 'Time for' reads as one phrase asking whether the moment has come, which hides the fact that the first word is working on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Seconds are the units a clock counts, and seconds at the table are a further helping of what has just been served.

entries.clue: Used keys again and went back in (2-7)

blocks.note: typed the figures a second time, at a keyboard
walked into the place a second time

annotation.surface: Somebody who worked the keys once more and then went back inside.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves hang on the same two-letter prefix, which is why the enumeration gives away more than the setter might like: two letters, a hyphen, then a word. The keys are the ones under the fingers, not the ones on a ring.
annotation.definitionFit: To re-enter figures is to key them in again after a first attempt, and to re-enter a building is simply to go back inside it.

entries.clue: A bit posh or synthetically, affectedly refined in speech (5)

indicatorNotes.A bit: a bit of something is a part of it and never the whole, so only a few of the letters that follow are wanted

blocks.note: the run starts on the last letter of the first word, swallows the short one whole and stops two letters into the last

annotation.surface: A verdict on someone posh, or only pretending to be, and the voice that gives them away.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden runs like to sit across the join between two long words, and a short word such as 'or' is exactly the join the eye skates over. 'A bit posh' reads as one judgement and is an instruction followed by its material.
annotation.definitionFit: Horsy is said of the county hunting set and, by extension, of the braying, over-genteel voice associated with them.

entries.clue: Say Oscar first in command, being self-obsessed (8)

blocks.note: e.g. introduces an example, which is the job 'say' does in a sentence
Oscar stands for O in the radio alphabet pilots and soldiers spell with
first written as 1st, with the figure read as the Roman one
i/c is the standard shorthand for the officer in charge of something

annotation.surface: Oscar promoted to the top of the chain of command and letting it go to his head.
annotation.walkthrough: Four abbreviations run together with nothing between them, so the difficulty is deciding where each one stops. 'Oscar' is the radio alphabet letter rather than the statuette the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone egoistic puts themselves at the centre of everything, which is what being self-obsessed describes.

entries.clue: Accursed rabid hound turns up (6)

indicatorNotes.turns up: in a down entry what turns up is read from the bottom of the column, so the letters arrive in the opposite order to the one they were built in

blocks.note: a rabid animal is a mad one
a hound is a dog

annotation.surface: A rabid dog turning up where it is not wanted.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the rabid hound are three letters long, so the seam between them is invisible until the whole thing is read back up the column. What comes up is an oath rather than an animal.
annotation.definitionFit: Goddam is the curse muttered over something, so whatever is goddam is accursed — damned by whoever is complaining about it.

entries.clue: Desecration of New Age relics (9)

indicatorNotes.New: what is made new is no longer what it was, so the letters beside it are to be rebuilt in another arrangement

blocks.note: nine letters for the mix, and the capital on the first is the surface's doing

annotation.surface: The desecration of relics belonging to some New Age faith.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New Age' is one phrase to the eye and two jobs in the parse, the first word shuffling everything after it. Nine-letter anagram material rarely announces itself this quietly.
annotation.definitionFit: Sacrilege is the violation of something held sacred, and desecration is the same offence named from the other side: treating holy things as ordinary.

entries.clue: Relative having base in Riviera location (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts one piece within another, so the letter named before it goes inside the word named after

blocks.note: Nice is the city on the French Riviera
e is the base of natural logarithms, the mathematician's constant

annotation.surface: A relative with a place on the French Riviera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' is the mathematician's constant, not the bottom of anything and not a military one. The Riviera town has to be taken as a proper name rather than as a description of somewhere pleasant.
annotation.definitionFit: A niece is your brother's or sister's daughter, a relative in the plain family sense the clue uses.

entries.clue: Consumes American drink round back of roadhouse (4,2)

indicatorNotes.round: what goes round something closes on both sides of it, so the pieces named before it end up either side of the letter named after
indicatorNotes.back of: the back of a word is the letter it ends on, and no more of it than that is wanted

blocks.note: US is the standard short form for American
to sup is to drink, a verb still in everyday use in the north of England
the letter the word ends on, as the instruction before it asks

annotation.surface: Somebody putting away an American drink at the back of a roadhouse.
annotation.walkthrough: The (4,2) split does not fall where the pieces do: it cuts through the last chunk, which is why the assembled letters are so hard to read back as two words. 'Round' is the only word saying the two short pieces separate.
annotation.definitionFit: To use something up is to consume the whole of it and leave none, which is the sense of 'consumes' here.

entries.clue: Farewell toast (7)

blocks.note: the cheerful goodbye called from a doorway
the word said over raised glasses

annotation.surface: A drink raised to somebody who is leaving.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words in the clue leave room for nothing but two definitions. Both senses are the same British exclamation, one at the door and one over a glass, which is why the pair reads as a single phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheerio is the informal British goodbye, and the same word was long called out as a drinking toast in the way 'cheers' is now.

entries.clue: Starts to dream up musical title (7)

indicatorNotes.Starts to: the start of a word is the letter it opens with, and the plural asks for one from each of the two words that follow

blocks.note: the opening letters of the two words, one from each
Chess is the 1984 musical by the two men of Abba with Tim Rice, set at a cold-war championship

annotation.surface: Somebody beginning to invent a title for a musical.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective attached to the word after it and is a noun naming one show in particular. The title wanted is the aristocratic sort rather than a name on a poster.
annotation.definitionFit: A duchess is the title held by a duke's wife, the rank immediately below a princess in the British peerage.

entries.clue: Crazy upper-class twit discharged in US city (5)

indicatorNotes.discharged: a load discharged has been emptied out, and a word emptied out keeps only the letters at its two ends
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the letters named before it inside the one named after

blocks.note: NY is New York, and its two letters part company to take the rest between them
U is the long-standing shorthand for upper-class
the two ends of the word, its middle discharged

annotation.surface: An upper-class idiot thrown out of a bar in an American city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discharged' reads as a sacking and is an emptying instruction. U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, the 1950s British parlour game of which words give your background away.
annotation.definitionFit: Nutty is the everyday word for crazy — a nutty idea or a nutty neighbour is one nobody is taking seriously.

entries.clue: 10 had, in essence, acquired a reputation for dishonesty (9)

indicatorNotes.acquired: what a phrase has acquired it now holds inside it, so the letters wanted are sitting somewhere in the words named before

blocks.note: the run begins on the last letter of the answer at 10 across, takes the two short words whole and stops three letters into the last

annotation.surface: Whoever is named at 10 across having, essentially, got themselves a name for dishonesty.
annotation.walkthrough: A cross-reference usually hands over a whole word; this one contributes a single letter from the end of the other answer and lets the clue's own words carry the run on. 'In essence' reads as a qualifier and is over half the hiding place.
annotation.definitionFit: Shadiness is the quality of looking as though one cannot be trusted, which is a reputation for dishonesty rather than proof of any.

entries.clue: Gloria's arranged housing for eastern women here (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a singular noun and 'women here' a phrase naming who is inside: the setter defines the building by its occupants, pointing at the place rather than naming it.

indicatorNotes.arranged: letters that have been arranged have been put in an order somebody chose, which need not be the one they came in
indicatorNotes.housing: to house something is to give it a place inside, so the letters being shuffled take the one named next in among them

blocks.note: seven letters for the mix, the apostrophe contributing nothing
E is the compass abbreviation for eastern, and the eighth letter of the mix

annotation.surface: Gloria has sorted out accommodation for some women from the east.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gloria's arranged' is the shuffle and 'housing' is what lets the compass letter into it. A seraglio is the women's quarters of a Muslim household, so the clue ends by pointing at the place instead of naming it.
annotation.definitionFit: A seraglio is the women's quarters of an Ottoman or Muslim household, so indicating where the women are indicates the building itself.

entries.clue: Top grub (as cooked here?) (9)

indicatorNotes.cooked: what has been cooked is no longer in its raw state, so the letters beside it come to the table in a different order

blocks.note: seven letters for the mix, and the food the place is proud of
the little word joins the mix and brings the count to nine

annotation.surface: A boast that the food is the best and that it is cooked on the premises.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word works twice over, as material for the shuffle and as a plain description of the place. 'As' looks like grammar holding the sentence together and is two of the nine letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a gastropub is a pub that makes its name on food cooked to a standard well above ordinary pub grub.

entries.clue: Renovate equipment used to broadcast sermon? (6)

blocks.note: the sermon is the Rev's to give, and Rev is how the title is written in front of his name
an amp is what carries a voice to the back of a hall

annotation.surface: Kit for putting a sermon out to the congregation, or over the air.
annotation.walkthrough: The two chunks together make a piece of equipment nobody sells — the amplifier a clergyman plugs in — and the question mark is the setter admitting it. 'Renovate' at the front is the one straight word in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to do it up and put it back into service, which is renovating it.

entries.clue: Philosopher Ayer cleaned out horrid toilets (9)

indicatorNotes.cleaned out: a room cleaned out has had everything inside carried away and only its two walls left, which is what a word keeps at each end
indicatorNotes.horrid: something horrid is in a bad state, and letters in a bad state are letters out of their proper order

blocks.note: the two ends of the name, its middle cleaned away; A. J. Ayer was the British logical positivist
seven letters for the mix, joining the two already taken

annotation.surface: The philosopher A. J. Ayer scrubbing out some disgusting lavatories.
annotation.walkthrough: One philosopher's name supplies the opening of another's, which is the joke the surface is built to hide. 'Cleaned out' does the emptying that 'horrid' looks better suited to, and 'horrid' does the shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: Aristotle is the Greek philosopher, Plato's pupil and Alexander's tutor, so the plain word names him without any stretch.

entries.clue: Lover boy turned on as sparkling wine goes round (8)

indicatorNotes.turned: what is turned faces the other way, so the two short words after it are read back to front
indicatorNotes.goes round: what goes round a thing sits on both sides of it, so the word named before splits to take the rest inside

blocks.note: cava is the Spanish fizz made by the champagne method
the two little words read backwards, as the instruction in front of them asks

annotation.surface: A boy turned on as the fizz goes round the room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as one phrase and breaks in the middle: the first word is the instruction and the second is the first thing it acts on. The wine's four letters then part in the centre to take the reversal inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A Casanova is a man with a long list of conquests, named after the eighteenth-century Venetian memoirist, which is exactly the lover boy type.

entries.clue: Most vulgar ways in France and the UK to frame Germany? (6)

indicatorNotes.to frame: a frame goes round what it holds, so the pieces named before it close on the letter named after

blocks.note: a rue is a street in France
St is how a street is written on a British address
D is Germany's international vehicle plate, for Deutschland

annotation.surface: The coarsest methods France and Britain might use to pin the blame on Germany.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frame' in a sentence about one country and two others wants to be a stitch-up, and is the container instruction. The question mark covers a plate letter that names the country only to a driver.
annotation.definitionFit: Rudest is the superlative of rude, and to be rude is to be coarse or vulgar in what you say and do.

entries.clue: Stop bucketin' down, by the sound of it (4,2)

indicatorNotes.by the sound of it: it asks for what the words sound like when said aloud, not for how they are spelt

blocks.note: to bucket down is British for raining hard, and the dropped g in the clue asks for the same clipped pronunciation of the word for it

annotation.surface: A plea for the downpour to stop.
annotation.walkthrough: The dropped g is the whole instruction: the clipped word for heavy rain is what the answer sounds like, spelt as two quite different words. 'Stop' at the front reads as part of the complaint.
annotation.definitionFit: To rein in is to pull a horse up on the reins, and so to stop anything that is running away with itself.

entries.clue: Confront newspaper defending large international operation (4-4)

indicatorNotes.defending: what defends something stands around it, so the two pieces named before close on the letters named after

blocks.note: to face a problem is to confront it
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink London business daily
L is the clothing-size letter for large
I is the usual single letter for international

annotation.surface: A newspaper standing up for a big international operation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Operation' at the end is the surgical kind, not the military one the rest of the sentence builds towards. What does the defending is two separate pieces, one at each end, with the large international pair shut between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A face-lift is the cosmetic operation that tightens the skin of the face, so 'operation' is the plain medical word for it.

entries.clue: Everybody featured in trial least likely to be believable (7)

indicatorNotes.featured in: what features in something appears inside it, so the word named before goes within the one named after

blocks.note: a test is a trial
all is everybody, the whole of them

annotation.surface: Everyone named in a court case, and not one of them convincing.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the sense the word has in 'a tall story', nothing to do with height, which is where the surface leaves you looking. A four-letter word opens after its first letter to take the other one inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A tall story is one stretched past belief, so the tallest is the one least likely to be believed — a sense that survives mainly in that phrase.

entries.clue: Ogilvie regularly disembarked the German aircraft (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly disembarked: to disembark is to get off, and letters getting off at regular intervals leave every other one still aboard

blocks.note: the second letter of the name and every other one after it, the rest having got off
der is one of the German words for 'the'

annotation.surface: A man who regularly got off a German aircraft.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The German' is a phrase with a translation hidden in it, the German for 'the'. 'Regularly' is the usual signal for every other letter, and 'disembarked' names the ones that leave rather than the ones that stay.
annotation.definitionFit: A glider is an aircraft with no engine, held up by rising air alone, so the general word covers it.

entries.clue: Bury the greatest article along with the rest (5,4)

blocks.note: to inter a body is to bury it
Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest, and most of the world came round to it
a is the indefinite article

annotation.surface: Burying the greatest of them along with everything else.
annotation.walkthrough: The boxer is the only proper name in the clue and it arrives without a capital, which is what makes him hard to see. Latin tags like this one belong to legal writing, where the remainder of a list goes unsaid.
annotation.definitionFit: Inter alia is Latin for 'among other things', written to show that what has just been named came along with the rest of a longer list.

entries.clue: Experience Rubens' final piece hung in gallery (5)

indicatorNotes.final piece: the final piece of a name is the letter it ends on, though in a clue about painters it reads as a last canvas
indicatorNotes.hung in: a painting hung in a gallery is inside it, so the letter goes within the word named after

blocks.note: the Tate is the London gallery of British and modern art, now four of them
the letter the painter's name ends on

annotation.surface: A last work by Rubens hanging in a gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs in an art gallery, including the two that turn out to be instructions. The Flemish painter is there for the single letter his name ends on.
annotation.definitionFit: To taste freedom or taste defeat is to experience it, the verb used of anything undergone rather than only of food.

entries.clue: Complete write off (5)

blocks.note: said of something whole, with nothing left out
what an insurer does to a car too badly damaged to repair

annotation.surface: A car declared a complete write-off.
annotation.walkthrough: The two definitions run into each other so smoothly that the clue looks like one phrase about a wreck. One half is an adjective and the other a verb, which is the only seam there is.
annotation.definitionFit: A total failure is a complete one, and to total a car is to write it off, the American verb that followed the insurance noun into British use.

entries.clue: St Paul's correspondent periodically rejected this truism (5)

indicatorNotes.periodically rejected: letters rejected at regular intervals leave the ones standing between them, which is every other letter of the words that follow

blocks.note: the first letter of the phrase and every other one after it, the rejected letters falling between

annotation.surface: Paul's correspondent now and then dismissing a well-worn saying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' is the every-other-letter signal and 'rejected' names the ones thrown away rather than the ones kept, which comes to the same count either way. The New Testament letter to Titus is addressed to the man Paul left in charge of the church in Crete.
annotation.definitionFit: Titus received one of Paul's New Testament letters, which makes him the apostle's correspondent in the plain sense of the man written to.

entries.clue: Tasteless, fashionable drink Ingrid drained (7)

indicatorNotes.drained: a glass drained has had everything inside taken out of it, so a word drained keeps only the letters at its two ends

blocks.note: what is in is what is fashionable
a sip is a small drink
the two ends of the name, the middle drained away

annotation.surface: Ingrid finishing a fashionable drink to the last drop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drained' belongs to the drinking picture and is the emptying instruction, which is the neatest turn in the clue. A comma is all that separates the definition from the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Something insipid has no flavour and, said of company or writing, no interest either — which is what tasteless covers in both senses.

entries.clue: Old court letter exposed Group of Eight (7)

indicatorNotes.exposed: a thing exposed has had its covering taken off, so the word loses the letter at each end and hands over what was underneath

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
Ct is how court is written in a street address
the word with its covering letters taken off

annotation.surface: An old court document that laid a group of eight bare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is the word itself on the page, not a letter of the alphabet and not one through the post, which is the step that takes longest to see. The capitals on the definition suggest a summit of nations.
annotation.definitionFit: An octette is a group of eight — eight singers or players, or the piece of music written for them.

entries.clue: Starmer bans me getting involved; shame (13)

indicatorNotes.getting involved: things that get involved with one another end up tangled together, and tangled letters are letters out of their order

blocks.note: thirteen letters for the mix, everything in the clue up to the semicolon

annotation.surface: The Prime Minister barring somebody from taking any part.
annotation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the British prime minister, and his surname plus two short words is thirteen letters of raw material. 'Getting involved' reads as the thing being forbidden and is the shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: An embarrassment is a source of shame, the awkward sort nobody wants to be associated with.
